peer_results.rationale: AMD's candidates focus on acquisition integration risks (amd_2024_1A_D091) and competitive practices of Intel (amd_2024_1A_D034). These topics do not relate to the risks of standard-essential patent licensing challenges, royalty collection limitations, or SEP enforcement remedies that define Qualcomm's disclosure.

AVGO's candidates focus on the integration risks of the VMware merger (avgo_2024_1A_D044) and general M&A/divestiture risks (avgo_2024_1A_D045). These concern acquisition execution and licensing model transitions (perpetual to subscription) but do not address the specific legal/regulatory challenges to intellectual property royalty collection or standard-essential patent enforcement faced by Qualcomm.

comparisons.peer_topic: Intellectual Property Protection and Enforcement Risks
comparisons.peer_summary: Intel faces risks in protecting and enforcing its IP rights due to litigation, varying enforceability, and geopolitical factors, including compulsory licensing. Additionally, licensing practices and industry standard participation may allow competitors to use patents or exhaust rights, impairing IP value.
comparisons.comparison: Both Qualcomm and Intel disclose risks related to the protection and enforcement of their intellectual property rights, specifically highlighting the potential for adverse litigation outcomes and the difficulty of maintaining competitive advantage through IP. Qualcomm warns that challenges to its standard-essential patent (SEP) licensing model could limit its ability to collect royalties or seek injunctions, thereby harming its business model and revenues. Similarly, Intel acknowledges that its inability to enforce its IP rights can harm its competitive position, and that asserting IP rights may result in counter-claims. While Qualcomm focuses on the structural threats to its royalty-based business model from regulatory/legal challenges, Intel focuses on the general risk of IP theft, unauthorized use, and enforcement failures.

sentences.text: We expect that such proposals, interpretations and strategies will continue in the future, and if successful, our business model would be harmed, either by limiting or eliminating our ability to collect royalties (or by reducing the royalties we can collect) on all or a portion of our standard-essential patent portfolio, limiting our return on investment with respect to new technologies, limiting our ability to seek injunctions against infringers of our standard-essential patents, constraining our ability to make licensing commitments when submitting our technologies for inclusion in future standards (which could make our technologies less likely to be included in such standards) or forcing us to work outside of SDOs or other industry groups to promote our new technologies, and our revenues, results of operations and cash flows could be negatively impacted.
In addition, the legal and other costs associated with asserting or defending our positions have been and may in the future be significant.
Our assertion of IP rights may result in another party seeking to assert claims against us, which could harm our business.
Our inability to enforce our IP rights under any of these circumstances can harm our competitive position and business.

In addition, the theft or unauthorized use or publication of our trade secrets and other confidential business information could harm our competitive position and reduce acceptance of our products; as a result, the value of our investment in R&D, product development, and marketing could be reduced.
